start.title: Start here: Docker and Compose
start.description: Start with one app in one container. Then build its image, connect it to another app, keep its data, and manage both with Compose. An image is a packaged…
start.html:
Start with one app in one container. Then build its image, connect it to another app, keep its data, and manage both with Compose.

The big idea
An image is a packaged recipe. A container is one running—or stopped—instance. Compose is a file describing a group of containers and how they connect.

No prior Docker knowledge is required. Read the main lesson first; expand Common traps when you are ready. Code blocks are examples until the hands-on lesson.

1 · Meet containers · lessons 1–3Tell images and containers apart. Run, stop, start, and remove a pretend container.
2 · Build and share · lessons 4–7Understand Dockerfiles, caching, build stages, tags, registries, and CPU architectures.
3 · Run reliably · lessons 8–13Practice networking and storage; learn config, processes, health, security, and debugging.
4 · Compose · lessons 14–18Describe a stack, wait for readiness, change settings, recreate services, and recognize single-host limits.
5 · Build and recover · lessons 19–22Run a real two-service app, back up and restore it, then connect this knowledge to Kubernetes and Helm.

Finish line: rebuild the app from its files, diagnose a connection problem, recreate it without losing saved data, and restore a backup. Learn one or two lessons per sitting.

model.title: Image, container, and Docker Engine
model.description: Your app works on your laptop but fails on another computer because the files, libraries, or setup differ. An image bundles the app and its userspace…
model.html:
The problem
Your app works on your laptop but fails on another computer because the files, libraries, or setup differ.
The big idea
An image bundles the app and its userspace dependencies. Docker Engine creates containers from images. Containers isolate processes and share the host kernel; they are not each a full virtual machine.
Dockerfile→Build an image→Run containers

The Docker CLI sends requests to the daemon/Engine. A registry stores images for sharing. On a Mac, Linux containers normally run inside a Linux VM managed by Docker Desktop or another compatible runtime.

Common traps and useful edge cases

A container still needs compatible OS and CPU support. Docker context selects an Engine; it may be remote. Bind-mount paths refer to the daemon’s host, not necessarily your laptop.

Remember
  • Image = packaged filesystem and defaults. Container = an instance with its own writable layer.
  • Building, pulling, and running are separate actions.

quiz.q: Two containers use one image. Do they share all writable files automatically?
quiz.why: Each has its own writable layer unless you explicitly share storage.

quiz.q: Where do Linux containers run on a typical Mac Docker Desktop setup?
quiz.why: This explains some networking and filesystem differences from native Linux.

life.title: Run, stop, start, remove
life.description: run creates a new container. start starts an existing stopped one. Stop keeps its writable layer; removal deletes that layer. A stopped container also keeps…
life.html:
docker run -d --name pizza-demo -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 nginx:1.28
docker ps
docker stop pizza-demo
docker ps -a
docker start pizza-demo
docker rm -f pizza-demo

run creates a new container. start starts an existing stopped one. Stop keeps its writable layer; removal deletes that layer. A stopped container also keeps its name.

Practice safely in the browser

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • --rm removes the container after it exits; do not store important data in its writable layer.
  • A container stops when its main process exits. -d detaches your terminal; it does not keep a finished process alive.
  • exec runs a command inside a running container. attach attaches to its main process; input or signals can affect it.

quiz.q: After stop then start, does the same container keep its writable files?
quiz.why: Removal or replacement discards that layer, not an ordinary stop/start.

file.title: Read and write a Dockerfile
file.description: FROM selects a base. WORKDIR sets a directory. COPY adds files from the build context. RUN executes during the build. USER selects the runtime user. CMD…
file.html:
📄 Our small Dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --create-home appuser \
    && mkdir -p /data && chown appuser:appuser /data
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser app.py ./app.py
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

FROM selects a base. WORKDIR sets a directory. COPY adds files from the build context. RUN executes during the build. USER selects the runtime user. CMD supplies the default startup command.

docker build -t pizza:dev .
# the dot is the build context, not just the Dockerfile location
📄 .dockerignore keeps unwanted context out
.git
.env
.env.*
*.db
__pycache__
*.pyc
Common traps and useful edge cases

EXPOSE 8000 documents a port; it does not publish it to your laptop. A later RUN export X=1 does not create persistent runtime config; use ENV or runtime environment settings. Files outside the build context cannot simply be copied with ../.

options: Whenever a container receives a request
quiz.why: CMD or ENTRYPOINT controls runtime startup.

cache.title: Build cache: what must run again?
cache.description: Docker can reuse unchanged build steps. Put slow dependency installation before frequently changing source files, when your project allows it.
cache.html:
The big idea
Docker can reuse unchanged build steps. Put slow dependency installation before frequently changing source files, when your project allows it.
📄 Example for a Python app with dependencies
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

Practice safely in the browser

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • Changing an earlier step invalidates dependent later steps in that stage.
  • --no-cache rebuilds steps; use --pull when you also want a refreshed base tag.
  • A remote package repository changing does not itself change the text of a cached RUN step. Pin dependencies and rebuild deliberately.
  • BuildKit cache mounts speed downloads without making the cache part of the final image. Cache is disposable, not a backup.

quiz.q: Source changes, dependency file stays the same. A well-ordered build can…
quiz.why: Copying source after installing dependencies limits needless rebuilds.

stages.title: Build stages, secrets, and small images
stages.description: A multi-stage build uses one stage to compile or prepare artifacts, then copies only what runtime needs into another stage. This pattern needs a compatible…
stages.html:
The big idea
A multi-stage build uses one stage to compile or prepare artifacts, then copies only what runtime needs into another stage.
📄 The pattern, not a complete app
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app .

FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
USER 10001:10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

This pattern needs a compatible static binary. Real apps may also need CA certificates, timezone data, or other runtime files. A tiny image that cannot do its job is not an improvement.

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • Do not pass build credentials through ARG, ENV, or COPY. Use BuildKit secret/SSH mounts, and ensure your build command does not print or copy the secret.
  • Deleting a copied secret in a later layer does not erase it from earlier image layers.
  • Minimal/distroless images may have no shell. Debug with logs, inspect, or a suitable debug image rather than assuming sh exists.
docker build --secret id=token,src=./token.txt .
# Dockerfile consumes it during one step:
# RUN --mount=type=secret,id=token your-tool --token-file /run/secrets/token

registry.title: Tags, digests, registries, and platforms
registry.description: Replace YOUR_USER with your registry namespace. A tag is a movable name; a digest identifies immutable content. Pulling a newer image does not replace…
registry.html:
docker tag pizza:dev YOUR_USER/pizza:v1
docker login
docker push YOUR_USER/pizza:v1
docker pull YOUR_USER/pizza:v1

Replace YOUR_USER with your registry namespace. A tag is a movable name; a digest identifies immutable content. Pulling a newer image does not replace already-running containers.

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • latest is just a tag; it is not a freshness guarantee.
  • Apple Silicon commonly uses arm64; many servers use amd64. An exec format error may indicate the wrong architecture or an invalid executable script.
  • docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t YOUR_USER/pizza:v1 . publishes a multi-platform image when your builder supports it. Emulation can be slower.
  • Pin release images, scan them, and rebuild for fixes. Pinning a digest improves reproducibility but does not apply future security updates automatically.

quiz.q: You pull a new version of a tag. What happens to a running container?
options: It keeps its current image until replaced
quiz.why: A running container does not change its image under its feet.

network.title: Ports, localhost, and service names
network.description: A published port maps a host address/port to a container port. Inside a container, localhost refers to that container—not another service or your laptop.…
network.html:
The big idea
A published port maps a host address/port to a container port. Inside a container, localhost refers to that container—not another service or your laptop.
Laptop localhost:8080→Published port→web:8000→api:8000 on the shared network

Practice safely in the browser

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • The app generally needs to listen on 0.0.0.0 inside the container to accept connections arriving through its network interface.
  • -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8000 limits host publication to loopback. Omitting the host address commonly publishes on all interfaces.
  • Compose creates a project network with DNS service names. Use api:8000 between services, not the host-published port.
  • Two containers cannot bind the same host address/port. EXPOSE alone does not publish a port.
  • host.docker.internal is useful on Docker Desktop; native Linux may need explicit host-gateway configuration. Do not assume Desktop and Linux networking are identical.

quiz.q: From web, how do you call api on the same Compose network?
quiz.why: Use the service name and the port the app listens on inside its container.

storage.title: Writable layers, volumes, and bind mounts
storage.description: Storage Use it for Lifetime Writable container layer Disposable files Until that container is removed Named volume App/database data managed by Docker Until…
storage.html:
StorageUse it forLifetime
Writable container layerDisposable filesUntil that container is removed
Named volumeApp/database data managed by DockerUntil explicitly removed
Bind mountA chosen host path, often source codeThe host path has its own lifetime
tmpfsTemporary memory-backed filesNot persistent after the container stops

Practice safely in the browser

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • A mount hides files already present at its target path; they may not be gone from the image.
  • Linux permissions use numeric UIDs/GIDs. A non-root container may not be allowed to write a host directory.
  • Use read-only bind mounts when writing is unnecessary. Mounting a host directory can let the container modify host files.
  • A named volume is not a backup and does not automatically replicate to another machine.
  • A new empty volume can receive existing image contents at the mount target; an existing volume keeps its old contents.

quiz.q: You remove a container using a named volume. Is that volume automatically erased?
quiz.why: Volume deletion is separate; Compose down -v can remove its project volumes.

config.title: Config and secrets at build time and runtime
config.description: ARG supplies build-time input. ENV defines an image environment default. docker run -e and Compose environment configure a container when it is created. Use…
config.html:
ARG supplies build-time input. ENV defines an image environment default. docker run -e and Compose environment configure a container when it is created.

docker run --rm -e MENU_SIZE=large pizza:dev
# A real app must read MENU_SIZE for this setting to do anything.

Use secret files or an appropriate secret manager for sensitive values. Compose secrets can grant a service access to a file under /run/secrets/; the app must read it. Local Compose secrets do not by themselves create an encrypted vault.

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • Environment variables may be visible to people with container-inspection access and may appear in diagnostics.
  • .env is not a secret store, and .dockerignore is not the same as .gitignore. Keep credentials out of both image context and git.
  • Changing an environment file does not update an already-created container. Recreate it with the new configuration.

process.title: Main process, shutdown, health, and restart
process.description: Docker tracks the main process. Health checks add a separate signal about whether the app works. Running and healthy are different states. docker stop sends…
process.html:
The big idea
Docker tracks the main process. Health checks add a separate signal about whether the app works. Running and healthy are different states.
📄 Prefer exec-form startup
ENTRYPOINT ["python"]
CMD ["app.py"]

docker stop sends a stop signal, then force-kills after the grace period if necessary. Your app should handle signals and close work cleanly. init: true in Compose helps forward signals and reap orphaned child processes.

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • Plain Docker restart policies react to process exit. An unhealthy status alone does not automatically restart a running container.
  • restart: unless-stopped is not a fix for bad config, and it does not undo an intentional stop.
  • Arguments after an image name replace its CMD defaults; ENTRYPOINT usually remains. Compose command and entrypoint override different parts of startup. Inspect both when a container runs the wrong command.
  • Exec-form command arguments are not expanded by a shell. Shell-form entrypoints can complicate signal delivery; if you need a wrapper, end it with exec.
  • A dependency becoming healthy once does not mean it will stay available. Apps still need timeouts, retries, and reconnection logic.

quiz.q: A running container turns unhealthy. Will plain Docker necessarily restart it?
quiz.why: A health check is a health signal, not a universal restart controller.

security.title: Permissions, resources, and safe defaults
security.description: Use a non-root user where the app supports it. Check volume ownership. Avoid --privileged, host namespaces, and mounting the Docker socket unless you…
security.html:
• Use a non-root user where the app supports it. Check volume ownership.
  • Avoid --privileged, host namespaces, and mounting the Docker socket unless you understand the access they grant.
  • Drop unneeded capabilities; use read-only filesystems and writable tmpfs/volumes where appropriate.
  • Set reasonable memory/CPU limits and test behavior under them.
  • Use maintained images, rebuild for patches, and minimize exposed host ports.
Common traps and useful edge cases

Rootless Engine and a non-root container user are different layers of protection. Never treat container isolation as permission to run untrusted code with powerful host mounts. On many Linux setups, access to a rootful Docker daemon is effectively host-administrator access. A memory limit can lead to OOM termination; exit 137 alone is not proof—inspect OOMKilled. CPU limiting generally slows work rather than killing it.

docker stats
docker inspect --format "{{.State.OOMKilled}}" pizza-demo

debug.title: Debug first, clean up carefully
debug.description: First ask: did it exit, is it unhealthy, or is it simply unreachable? Then inspect logs, command, environment, mounts, network, and port mapping. exec needs…
debug.html:
docker ps -a
docker logs --tail 100 pizza-demo
docker inspect pizza-demo
docker exec -it pizza-demo sh
docker stats
docker system df

First ask: did it exit, is it unhealthy, or is it simply unreachable? Then inspect logs, command, environment, mounts, network, and port mapping. exec needs a running container and the requested program must exist inside it.

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • Name already in use: inspect docker ps -a; a stopped container still has its name.
  • Port allocated: another container or host process is using that address/port.
  • No space left: inspect images, writable layers, volumes, build cache, and log size before deleting anything.
  • Write application logs to stdout/stderr so the configured logging driver can collect them. Files written inside the container do not automatically appear in docker logs. Limit/rotate logs so a noisy app cannot fill the disk.
  • Inspect first, remove named disposable resources second. Global prune commands can affect other projects; volumes may contain important data.
Remember
  • ps → logs → inspect → targeted fix.
  • Rebuild containers from images and config instead of relying on hand-edits inside them.

compose.title: Compose: one file for the whole app
compose.description: Compose describes services, networks, and volumes together. A service is the recipe for one app component; containers are the instances that run it. web…
compose.html:
The big idea
Compose describes services, networks, and volumes together. A service is the recipe for one app component; containers are the instances that run it.
📄 Our complete compose.yaml
name: pizza-learning
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      DB_PATH: /data/pizza.db
    volumes:
      - pizza-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.5
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
  web:
    build: .
    environment:
      UPSTREAM: http://api:8000
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8000"
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.5
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
volumes:
  pizza-data:

web answers the browser and calls api. The API stores a counter in a named volume. Only web publishes a host port. Both join the project network and use DNS service names.

docker compose config
docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail 50
Common traps and useful edge cases

Use the modern docker compose command. Top-level version: is obsolete for current Compose. A project name scopes container/network/volume names; -p overrides the default. Reuse the same project name when you want the same data volume.

quiz.q: What does a Compose service describe?
options: A recipe/configuration for an app component
quiz.why: The word service has different meanings in Docker Compose and Kubernetes.

startup.title: Started is not ready
startup.description: Your web container starts immediately. The API is still preparing. The first request fails even though both containers say “running”. Short-form depends_on…
startup.html:
The problem
Your web container starts immediately. The API is still preparing. The first request fails even though both containers say “running”.
The big idea
Short-form depends_on orders startup. A health check plus condition: service_healthy waits for a dependency to pass its check before starting the dependent service.

Practice safely in the browser

Common traps and useful edge cases

This is startup coordination, not continuous supervision. If the API fails later, Compose does not automatically restart every dependent service. Apps must handle temporary failures. A successful health check only proves what its check actually tested.

quiz.q: Short-form depends_on alone guarantees a database can answer queries?
quiz.why: Started does not necessarily mean ready; use a suitable health check and resilient app behavior.

compose-config.title: Compose values, overrides, profiles, and secrets
compose-config.description: Keep two different jobs clear: Compose interpolates {NAME} in the YAML, while a container gets environment variables through environment, env_file, or image…
compose-config.html:
Keep two different jobs clear: Compose interpolates ${NAME} in the YAML, while a container gets environment variables through environment, env_file, or image defaults.

📄 Example fragment
services:
  web:
    image: "myapp:${TAG:-dev}"
    environment:
      LOG_LEVEL: "${LOG_LEVEL:-info}"
    env_file: runtime.env

A project .env file can supply interpolation values; its entries are not all automatically injected into the container. An explicit environment entry takes precedence over the same key from env_file. Use docker compose config to see the resolved configuration.

Common traps and useful edge cases
  • Shell variables can override interpolation defaults. Use --env-file intentionally and do not publish resolved config containing secrets.
  • Use $$ when a dollar sign should reach the container command rather than be expanded by Compose.
  • Multiple -f files merge by Compose rules; lists do not all behave like simple replacement. Inspect the result. Paths are normally relative to the first Compose file.
  • Quote values that YAML might interpret unexpectedly, including boolean-like strings and port mappings.
  • Profiles enable optional services: docker compose --profile tools up. Dependencies and explicitly targeted services need attention.

compose-life.title: Up, restart, recreate, down
compose-life.description: Command What to expect up -d Create/start services; recreate when required by changed configuration or image stop / start Stop/start existing containers;…
compose-life.html:
CommandWhat to expect
up -dCreate/start services; recreate when required by changed configuration or image
stop / startStop/start existing containers; preserve their writable layers
restartRestart existing containers; does not apply newly edited environment settings
up -d --buildBuild images and apply service configuration
up -d --force-recreateReplace containers even if config appears unchanged
downRemove project containers and networks; keep named volumes by default
down -vAlso remove declared project named volumes and attached anonymous volumes; external volumes are excluded
Common traps and useful edge cases

Removing a container is different from deleting its data volume. Anonymous volumes are harder to reattach reliably after replacement; use named volumes for persistent app data. Rebuilding an image alone is not the same as recreating the running service from it.

quiz.q: You changed environment in compose.yaml. Which applies it?
quiz.why: Restart does not reread new configuration into an existing container.

compose-scale.title: Development, scaling, and production limits
compose-scale.description: For development, bind mounts or Compose Watch can shorten the edit/build/run loop. For deployment, prefer a tested image and explicit configuration so the…
compose-scale.html:
For development, bind mounts or Compose Watch can shorten the edit/build/run loop. For deployment, prefer a tested image and explicit configuration so the result is reproducible.

docker compose exec web python --version
docker compose run --rm --no-deps web python --version
# exec uses an existing container; run creates a one-off container.
Common traps and useful edge cases
  • docker compose run does not publish the service’s ports by default; --service-ports opts in and may collide with running services.
  • --scale api=3 needs an app/data model that supports replicas. Do not scale our SQLite demo this way.
  • A fixed container_name prevents normal service scaling. Fixed host ports also collide across replicas.
  • Compose does not automatically supply a public load balancer or guaranteed zero-downtime rolling updates.
  • On a single Docker host, losing that host loses service availability. Restart policies do not provide multi-node failover.
  • For production, plan updates, TLS, backups, log rotation, alerts, and recovery. Compose is not a substitute for operating the host.

real.title: Build the real two-service app
real.description: Open a terminal only now. Install and start Docker Desktop or your chosen compatible Engine with Compose. This exercise is a small learning web server, not…
real.html:
Open a terminal only now. Install and start Docker Desktop or your chosen compatible Engine with Compose. This exercise is a small learning web server, not a production server.

docker version
docker compose version
docker context show

Use a new working folder for this exercise. The next command writes four files there.

cat > app.py <<'EOF'
import os
import signal
import sqlite3
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.request import urlopen

UPSTREAM = os.getenv("UPSTREAM", "")
DB_PATH = os.getenv("DB_PATH", "/data/pizza.db")
PORT = int(os.getenv("PORT", "8000"))
if not UPSTREAM:
    with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as db:
        db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS visits (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, count INTEGER NOT NULL)")
        db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO visits VALUES (1, 0)")

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        try:
            if self.path == "/healthz":
                body = b"healthy\n"
            elif self.path != "/":
                self.send_error(404)
                return
            elif UPSTREAM:
                with urlopen(UPSTREAM + "/", timeout=3) as response:
                    body = response.read()
            else:
                with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as db:
                    db.execute("UPDATE visits SET count = count + 1 WHERE id = 1")
                    count = db.execute("SELECT count FROM visits WHERE id = 1").fetchone()[0]
                body = ("Pizza visits: " + str(count) + "\n").encode()
            self.send_response(200)
        except Exception as error:
            print(type(error).__name__, flush=True)
            self.send_response(503)
            body = b"Backend unavailable. Check the api logs and UPSTREAM address.\n"
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

def stop(signum, frame):
    raise SystemExit(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, stop)
    with HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", PORT), Handler) as server:
        print("Listening on port", PORT, flush=True)
        server.serve_forever()
EOF
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.13-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
RUN useradd --uid 10001 --create-home appuser \
    && mkdir -p /data && chown appuser:appuser /data
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser app.py ./app.py
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "app.py"]
EOF
cat > .dockerignore <<'EOF'
.git
.env
.env.*
*.db
__pycache__
*.pyc
EOF
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
name: pizza-learning
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      DB_PATH: /data/pizza.db
    volumes:
      - pizza-data:/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.5
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
  web:
    build: .
    environment:
      UPSTREAM: http://api:8000
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8000"
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/healthz', timeout=2)"]
      interval: 3s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped
    init: true
    mem_limit: 128m
    cpus: 0.5
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
volumes:
  pizza-data:
EOF
What does this app do?

web proxies requests to api using its DNS name. api stores a visit counter in SQLite under /data. A GET to / intentionally increments the counter for this demo. The health endpoint does not increment it. The app uses Python’s standard library.

📄 app.py
import os
import signal
import sqlite3
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from urllib.request import urlopen

UPSTREAM = os.getenv("UPSTREAM", "")
DB_PATH = os.getenv("DB_PATH", "/data/pizza.db")
PORT = int(os.getenv("PORT", "8000"))
if not UPSTREAM:
    with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as db:
        db.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS visits (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, count INTEGER NOT NULL)")
        db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO visits VALUES (1, 0)")

class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        try:
            if self.path == "/healthz":
                body = b"healthy\n"
            elif self.path != "/":
                self.send_error(404)
                return
            elif UPSTREAM:
                with urlopen(UPSTREAM + "/", timeout=3) as response:
                    body = response.read()
            else:
                with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as db:
                    db.execute("UPDATE visits SET count = count + 1 WHERE id = 1")
                    count = db.execute("SELECT count FROM visits WHERE id = 1").fetchone()[0]
                body = ("Pizza visits: " + str(count) + "\n").encode()
            self.send_response(200)
        except Exception as error:
            print(type(error).__name__, flush=True)
            self.send_response(503)
            body = b"Backend unavailable. Check the api logs and UPSTREAM address.\n"
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(body)

def stop(signum, frame):
    raise SystemExit(0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, stop)
    with HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", PORT), Handler) as server:
        print("Listening on port", PORT, flush=True)
        server.serve_forever()

docker compose up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
curl http://localhost:8080
curl http://localhost:8080
docker compose exec web python -c "import urllib.request; print(urllib.request.urlopen('http://api:8000/').read().decode())"
docker compose up -d --force-recreate --wait api
curl http://localhost:8080

If port 8080 is busy, change only the host port in 127.0.0.1:8080:8000 and use that port in your browser. Keep the stack for the backup exercise next.

backup.title: Back up, restore, and remove only your lab
backup.description: A volume survives container replacement. A backup lets you recover when the volume or host is lost. Prove the backup works by restoring it. For this SQLite…
backup.html:
The big idea
A volume survives container replacement. A backup lets you recover when the volume or host is lost. Prove the backup works by restoring it.

For this SQLite demo, use SQLite’s backup API for a consistent copy. Other databases have their own dump/snapshot and restore procedures; do not blindly copy live database files.

docker compose exec -T api python -c "import sqlite3; src=sqlite3.connect('/data/pizza.db'); dst=sqlite3.connect('/tmp/pizza-backup.db'); src.backup(dst); dst.close(); src.close()"
docker compose cp api:/tmp/pizza-backup.db ./pizza-backup.db
docker compose stop api
docker compose run --rm --no-deps -v "$PWD/pizza-backup.db:/backup/pizza.db:ro" api python -c "import shutil; shutil.copyfile('/backup/pizza.db', '/data/pizza.db')"
docker compose up -d --wait
curl http://localhost:8080

The next visit should continue from the backed-up count. Store an additional copy outside this machine before depending on it.

docker compose down
Common traps and useful edge cases

When you deliberately want to erase the practice counter too, use docker compose down -v in this project. Keep the backup file. Do not use a global volume prune as a shortcut. Logs, images, and build cache have separate lifecycles and cleanup commands.

integration.title: How Docker connects to Kubernetes and Helm
integration.description: Dockerfile → image → Registry → Kubernetes Deployment uses the image → Helm packages the Kubernetes manifests Compose is useful for describing a local or…
integration.html:
Dockerfile → image→Registry→Kubernetes Deployment uses the image→Helm packages the Kubernetes manifests

Compose is useful for describing a local or single-host stack. Kubernetes introduces scheduling and reconciliation across a cluster. Helm packages and configures Kubernetes resources.

Docker / Compose ideaKubernetes counterpart to learn
ImageThe same compatible container image can be referenced in a Pod
Service processDeployment + Pod template
Service-name networkingService + cluster DNS
Named volumePVC + a suitable storage provider
Environment / secret fileConfigMap / Secret and access controls
Compose fileSeveral manifests; optionally packaged in a Helm chart

These are conceptual parallels, not a lossless file conversion. In particular, Kubernetes does not use Compose depends_on, and normal Kubernetes runtimes do not require Docker Engine. Review storage, health, retries, and networking when moving an app.

Remember
  • A useful learning order is Docker → Compose → Kubernetes → Helm.
  • Use the topic dropdown to continue; each topic keeps its own progress.

grad.html:
Use the two-service app as your final test. Tick a task only after you can do it and explain why it works.

You have reached the core finish line. Keep the Common traps notes as a reference, then move to the Kubernetes topic. Specialist topics such as custom storage drivers, GPU workloads, advanced networking, and Swarm deserve separate study when your project needs them.
